Weierstrass Approximation Theorem

Can polynomials alone imitate every continuous function on an interval?

A Bernstein polynomial averages the function's values near each point. As the degree grows, the average concentrates near that point. So the polynomial follows even the bumpy corners. The proof's fine estimates are only sketched.

For example, think of replacing a slope with a 🪜 staircase. The finer the steps, the smaller the gap anywhere you measure. Raising the degree presses the polynomial onto the whole function at once.

Bn(f)(x)=∑k=0nf ⁣(kn)(nk)xk(1−x)n−kB_n(f)(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} f\!\left(\frac{k}{n}\right) \binom{n}{k} x^k (1-x)^{n-k}Bn​(f)(x)=k=0∑n​f(nk​)(kn​)xk(1−x)n−k
f∈C[0,1]  ⟹  ∥Bn(f)−f∥∞→0f \in C[0,1] \implies \|B_n(f) - f\|_\infty \to 0f∈C[0,1]⟹∥Bn​(f)−f∥∞​→0

Prove that Bn(1)=1B_n(1) = 1Bn​(1)=1 — the constant function is reproduced exactly.

Bn(1)(x)=∑k=0n(nk)xk(1−x)n−k=(x+(1−x))n=1B_n(1)(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^k(1-x)^{n-k} = (x+(1-x))^n = 1Bn​(1)(x)=k=0∑n​(kn​)xk(1−x)n−k=(x+(1−x))n=1
Show proof

  1. Since f≡1f \equiv 1f≡1, we have f(k/n)=1f(k/n) = 1f(k/n)=1. Hence Bn(1)(x)=∑k=0n(nk)xk(1−x)n−kB_n(1)(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^k(1-x)^{n-k}Bn​(1)(x)=∑k=0n​(kn​)xk(1−x)n−k — just the sum of the basis functions.

  2. By the binomial theorem, ∑k=0n(nk)xk(1−x)n−k=(x+(1−x))n=1n=1\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^k(1-x)^{n-k} = (x + (1-x))^n = 1^n = 1∑k=0n​(kn​)xk(1−x)n−k=(x+(1−x))n=1n=1.

  3. So Bn(1)(x)=1B_n(1)(x) = 1Bn​(1)(x)=1 for every xxx and every nnn — zero error. The constant is not approximated; it is reproduced.
